#4083. Xbox Publisher Announces Four Games Being Delisted By End Of 2026

All set to disappear in a few weeks' time

It's never good news when games get delisted on the Xbox Store, but we haven't actually got many for the end of 2026 as things stand, and at least we're getting some notice on the four titles that are set to be removed.

All of these games are coming from one publisher - GameMill Entertainment. Their games can be very hit-and-miss, but most of them involve some pretty big IP, and I've enjoyed my time with a few of them in the past.

The four games they will be delisting on Xbox very soon are as follows:

The delist announcement for all four of these games was shared on Steam, and it only mentions Steam. However, GameMill has done this kind of thing before, and it's usually resulted in delistings for multiple platforms including Xbox.

As for whether they're worth it? Well, Avatar: The Last Airbender - Quest for Balance doesn't exactly have the best reputation, while childish platformer Hotel Transylvania 3 only fares slightly better. Street Outlaws 2 is considered the better of the two and certainly looks intriguing, but still has mixed impressions based on what we've seen.

Honestly, you shouldn't be buying any of these games at full price in our view, but it's worth keeping an eye out to see if they get heavy discounts before the end of 2026. Street Outlaws 1 and 2 have already been reduced by 90% on Steam ahead of their delistings, and we reckon the same thing might happen on Xbox in the near future.

#4082. Mouthwashing is getting a feature film adaptation from Sony and I need all of you to be normal about it whenever it comes out

I quite liked that there video game Mouthwashing. It had a lot to say about how corporations take advantage of their workers, it played around with character perspective to let you in on certain narrative threads and withhold others until they're taut enough to snap, and was short enough so that its misery didn't outstay its welcome. What I wasn't so fond of was much of the fandom response that came afterwards, which is why I am quite scared to say that it's getting a movie from Sony.

As shared by The Hollywood Reporter, Sony have acquired the feature film rights to Mouthwashing, attaching names both promising and apprehension inducing to it. It's being produced in part by Scott Derrickson, director of Sinister (which I liked well enough) and Doctor Strange (a wet fart sound of a movie). What is more interesting is that Karyn Kusama, director of the excellent cult classic Jennifer's Body, is attached to direct. Given the game's themes of sexual assault, which is putting it lightly, it's nice to see a woman in the director's seat.

YES, MOUTHWASHING MOVIE IS REALLY HAPPENING SOON™ You thought you could escape responsibility by turning off your console? Produced by Sony Pictures' Screen Gems and directed by Karyn Kusama.[image or embed]

The thing that loops me back around to fear is having Matt Manfredi and Phil Hay attached as writers; the pair have long worked together, but often on stinkers like Clash of the Titans, The Tuxedo, and R.I.P.D. At the very least the two of them and Kusama are frequent collaborators, having made The Invitation and Destroyer together (it probably helps that Hay and Kusama are married).

As with every single live action adaptation of a video game, I of course immediately feel that it is wholly unnecessary, and certainly think that's the case for Mouthwashing. It's a game that has minimal interactivity, much more of a walking sim than anything else. It also deeply relies on said interactivity, alongside its first-person perspective, so I'm not sure how well that would translate. And upsettingly, the game developed an uncomfortably intense fandom that has frequently treated the game's themes as a suggestion, prioritising skits and memes above a real reckoning with what it's doing. This leaves me afraid of a film adaptation. Perhaps I'll log off for the day whenever it comes out.

#4081. Baldur's Gate 3 custom campaign mod channels World of Warcraft with an adventure about undead former slaves fighting to reclaim a kingdom

From the creator of the Act Two Expansion mod which came out in September

The opening act of a Baldur's Gate 3 custom campaign mod which injects an adventure set in the World of Warcraft universe into Larian's RPG has been released. The mod, Forsaken, is another ambitious bit of work from a modder who recently expanded the second act of BG3's main story with a new region to explore before you head into the final chapter. This time, they've abandoned the D&Dverse for a tale of undead slaves rising up after being freed from serving a Lich King.

"You play as one of the Forsaken; an Undead who has recently awakened to find they are no longer slaves to the Lich King," modder SquallyDaBeanz wrote of Forsaken, their latest creation to release via Nexus Mods. "Now you must find your place in this new world alongside other freed Undead as you fight to reclaim the kingdom of Lordaeron. Hunt fierce beasts, explore forgotten ruins, end dark rituals, slay zealots, discover magical items, and more in this Custom Campaign for levels 1-5."

This campaign's setting is based on the Tirisfal Glades region seen in both World of Warcraft's classic and vanilla versions, with the mod being deliberately disconnected from the world of Baldur's Gate and SquallyDaBeanz even having aimed to emulate WOW's design philosophy. The initial release only features Forsaken's first act, but there's still plenty to do within that.

More than 20 quests await across a map that the modder said is designed to feel as expansive as World of Warcraft usually does, while offering a good deal of things to discover despite it not being as tightly packed with locations and secrets as vanilla BG3's professionally crafted locales. There are some towns, settlements, and dungeons to run across as you adventure with a party of up to three specially-built companions. The trio - a fighter named Darnell, a mage called Isabella and a cleric named Duesten - can be found in a charming-sounding place dubbed Deathknell Chapel. "The current implementation is temporary and exists purely to have a full party for combat encounters," SquallyDaBeanz noted of these companions. "A complete overhaul is in the works but I chose to put it off for a future update."

While there are NPCs and traders to chat with, the current version of the mod's quite heavily focused on combat and is fairly linear compared to vanilla BG3. Though, that has seemed to be the case with a lot of BG3 custom campaign mods I've covered thus far, especially those that are still works-in-progress like Forsaken.

Going forwards, SquallyDaBeanz hasn't provided an estimate as to when the mod'll be getting a second act, but has laid out some features they plan to add to the opening act in future. More quests, class dialogue, skill checks, items, and lore books are all on the to-do list, as well as adding idle animations and cutscenes for some NPCs.

If you fancy giving Forsaken a go, you'll need to nab its main file and install it with help from the instructions in the mod's description. Then, once you've enabled Forsaken via BG3's in-game mod manager found in the main menu, you'll need to start a new game to be whisked off to WOWville.

#4080. There are no more Assassin's Creed remakes in development, because Ubisoft are focused on Hexe, Invictus and "projects you haven't heard about yet"

They're still updating Black Flag Resynced, however, and bringing NG+ to Valhalla

Ubisoft have announced that they aren't working on any more Assassin's Creed remakes for the moment, despite learning a "tremendous amount" from Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced. Instead, it's all shoulders to the wheel for a thrilling future that contains witches, a stronger sense of narrative cohesion, and possibly some kind of Assassin's Creed Smash Bros equivalent. In the shorter term, Ubisoft are still adding things to both Resynced and Assassin's Creed Valhalla.

The news comes as part of a fireside chat from Jean Guesdon, head of content. After offering libations to Assassin's Creed's new leadership team - in particular Martin Schelling, former Assassin's Creed: Revelations producer and nowadays, head of brand – he shares the results of a survey about whatpeople currently want from Assassin's Creed at large. Ubisoft's three takeaways are that players would like them to communicate more, work harder to shore up Assassin's Creed's "unique identity", and create "a more coherent narrative that respects and expands Assassin's Creed's lore."

All of which is basically telling us nothing, though I'm interested to hear thoughts from old AC stalwarts about where the frame story of Assassin vs Templar has gone off the rails. I feel like "incoherent" is AC's default state and a significant part of its charm. Ubisoft are going to do further closed-doors workshops about the future of the series with certain big cheeses in the AC fanbase, via Discord.

The post includes news of changes to existing Assassin's Creeds. Black Flag Resynced has just been updated with a New Game+ mode, a "nightmare" difficulty setting, some takedown animations, and some fresh cosmetics. Resynced's older/younger sibling Assassin's Creed Valhalla is also getting a New Game+ mode, out 5th November, which introduces a new optional progression system, more resources for upgrades, a new gear quality level, a stash system, and some cosmetics.

There's a section on Codename Invictus, Ubisoft's unrevealed multiplayer Assassin's Creed project, which had a closed playtest featuring a new prototype a few months ago. Ubisoft say people like the PvP, parkour, map verticality, and range of AC characters.

"One piece of feedback came through clearly though: players saw great potential in the foundations but wanted more of the pillars that define Assassin's Creed," Guesdon writes. "The team spent the past months acting on it, and Invictus is now evolving in an exciting direction that better reflects those pillars while staying true to its multiplayer ambitions." I quite enjoyed Assassin's Creed's first efforts at multiplayer, in which players posed as NPCs on crowded maps, but as a Doubting Thomas, I also suspect Invictus is some kind of suffocating live service kraken. I suspect this is what the unnamed playtesters meant by wanting "more of the pillars".

I am more interested to hear about Codename Hexe, Ubisoft's other big forthcoming Creedojaunt, even though Clint Hocking is no longer working on it. It's reportedly a witch fable set during the time of the Holy Roman Empire. They'll be telling us more about that next year, Guesdon says.

Finally - well, apart from some flannel about the AC Netflix series and the series' 20th anniversary next year - there's a paragraph about remakes. "One thing we want to be transparent about today is that we currently have no other Assassin's Creed remake actively in development," Guesdon writes. "Our teams are already focused on the next chapter of Assassin's Creed titles, including projects you haven't heard about yet, featuring new settings and stories. But don't mistake that for a closed door. Like many of you, we love the idea of revisiting our classic titles, and we'll keep exploring opportunities to bring older titles back."

Some context for all this: Ubisoft recently made layoffs at Resynced studio Ubisoft Singapore, in the course of wider cost-cutting after an injection of funds from Tencent. In May, company boss Yves Guillemot told investors that the coming financial year would be a "low point", promising healthier returns from Assassin's Creed, Far Cry and Ghost Recon by early 2029.

I didn't play Resynced, and I'm mixed on remakes at large. I like remakes when they are effectively brand new games that happen to be retelling a familiar story, and having fun with it: games like Final Fantasy VII Rebirth, which are in ferocious dialogue with the original. But remakes that are just about stuffing the mechanics into Unreal Engine 5 and grafting on some progression and crafting mechanics? It's just feeding ash to the fire. What's your mileage?

#4079. Helldivers 2 boss can "absolutely see" making a game parody of generative AI, but it would need to be "quirky" rather than "doom-laden"

Arrowhead's chief creative officer Johan Pilestedt can well imagine the Helldivers studio developing a videogame that satirises or parodies today's generative AI technology. The game in question wouldn't be a Helldivers project, however, and Pilestedt says it would need to be relatively upbeat, rather than an exercise in feverish despair. This seems like a tall order right now, at least while Tim Sweeney still has access to Twitter.

"AI has been worth parodying since the ‘80s, and I can absolutely see a game where you’re stuck in a world with an AI overlord that’s basically a deity," Pilestedt told me during an interview on the company's future. "But the Automatons already cover our robot enemy needs in Helldivers 2, so if we went there, it would be a new title, and we’d want to frame it in a quirky, fun way rather than a doom-laden one."

The aim to keep things light is consistent, of course, with how Helldivers approaches satire. "Not everyone gets it, but plenty of players love playing along with the joke," Pilestedt commented elsewhere in our chatathon, with regard to how Helldivers portrays fascism. "The humor doesn't hide the message, it delivers it."

While robotic, Helldivers 2's Automatons aren't a commentary on generative AI. They're broadly a spoof of Soviet Russia, red star imagery and all, if Soviet Russia had happened to be populated by Terminators. Based on the secessionist planet of Cyberstan, the Automatons are led by a group of Cyborgs who are waging war partly out of revenge for Super Earth's efforts to "euthanise" them. Still, perhaps there's scope to patch in more present-day parallels and upgrade the Automatons from cosy T-1000 analogues into something redolent of, say, Krafton's plans to use game data for unpiloted weapon systems.

Any satire of genAI Arrowhead make would need to reckon with the fact that Arrowhead appear open to making use of the technology, within limits. “I find that anything that is [an] AI-related debate in the games industry ends up being on both ends of the spectrum," Arrowhead CEO Shams Jorjani told The Game Business in an interview last year. "Either we have Square Enix executives talking about 77% being automated through QA, or we have developers who feel that... the very fabric of their being is being threatened and therefore all AI is bad AI. Maybe could it be that reality is somewhere in the middle?"

Jorjani contrasted fears about job losses to generative AI with less anxious reaction to older automation middleware such as Simplygon, while conceding that Simplygon isn't on the same "massive scale" as generative AI tools. He also stressed that "we need to make sure that we're not stealing people's intellectual property and rights".

Pilestedt didn't share his own opinions about generative AI during our conversation - in his defence, I didn't ask for them specifically. He did, however, talk about why Arrowhead's current unannounced project isn't Helldivers 3 - briefly, they don't want to "reset" the momentum of Helldivers 2.

#4078. Rockstar developer union could end up over 1,600 workers strong and encompass nearly all UK staff below senior management, IWGB claim

Organisers say a successful vote would create "the biggest recognised union in the UK games sector"

As we've previously covered, a vote on recognition of a union made up of UK-based Rockstar Games devs is set to take place around GTA 6's console launch on November 19th. The Independent Workers of Great Britain (IWGB) union, whom the Rockstar staff are working with in their efforts to organise, have now revealed just how many workers the Rockstar could end up encompassing if the recognition vote is successful. It's not a small number.

As reported by Game File, when asked to put a number on their claim that the vote could result in "the biggest recognised union in the UK games sector", the IWGB said that the union’s bargaining unit would be made up of more than 1,600 workers. That, according to the union, is nearly everyone at Rockstar's UK studios below the director level. The director level's typically corpospeak for senior management, or the point at which you go from regular staff to the lowest rungs of the exec ladder which leads all the way up to the biggest of gold-plated desks.

Naturally, this UK Rockstar union won't include Rockstar staff based in other studios across the world, including the US and India. Recent reporting from Bloomberg cited Rockstar's total staff number as being over 4,700 people in 12 places across the globe.

The UK union recognition votes will be held from November 12th, a week before GTA 6's console launch, and November 26th.

"For me, this vote comes down to ensuring employees at Rockstar get honesty and openness surrounding the decisions that affect them," Rockstar Game Workers Union Committee Member Shanti Easton-Steel said in a press release issued by IWBG earlier this week. "When management choices are kept hidden, we can’t properly address issues like the gender pay gap, the uneven and ever-changing policies on overtime pay, or the concerns many co-workers hold around job security post-release."

Also set to come to a head around the time GTA 6 plops onto consoles is the employment tribunal which has seen Rockstar and the IWGB butt heads over the former's decision to fire 34 mostly UK-based staffers last year. Rockstar have accused the fired staff of risking the leaking of confidential info while posting on a Discord server set up by union organisers. The IWGB have accused Rockstar of being motivated by a desire to union bust.

#4077. Gears Of War: E-Day Is Bringing Back Legacy Maps, Modes And Skins For Season 2

And tomorrow they’re giving away a free General RAAM skin!

The Coalition kicked off Gears' 20th anniversary celebrations by reviving a classic Versus mode, introducing a new Horde mission, and adding a few extra bits and bobs to Gears of War: E-Day.

It might not have seemed like much, but reintroducing Guardian to Versus was an excellent callback to the mode's debut in Gears of War 2. The game's first season is coming to a close at the end of November, making way for E-Day's Season 2 content: Legacy.

Tomorrow, E-Day players can claim a free General RAAM skin for multiplayer. All you have to do is log in - that's it. Season 2 begins on December 1st, promising to bring back fan-favourite maps, modes and skins to "honour the greatest hits of Gears over 20 years".

"And beginning December 1, we launch our next Season – titled Legacy – which continues to honor the greatest hits of Gears over 20 years in our maps, modes and multiplayer skins. Season 2 not only brings back some fan favorites from the history of the franchise but lets us reimagine characters in ways we’ve always wanted to see them – like Solemn Memories Dom, whose character skin depicts him in the suit he’s wearing in the famous photo of him and Maria from Gears of War 2."

Does this mean we're going to see Kalona's version of Gridlock, Blood Drive and Canals? I sure hope so! I'd also like to reunite the Carmine family in E-Day. Can you imagine a full squad of Carmines voiced by the one and only Michael Gough? I can, and I want it!

@Fiendish-Beaver Whilst I agree with you about the next Gen, I don't think Consoles will last and they aren't really fulfilling the role they used to do.

Consoles were always the cheap mass market gaming device because Computers were too expensive. The Console was a 'kids' toy where teens/adults had Computers like Commodore 64 or Sinclair Spectrum but thanks to Sony pushing their Playstation to the young Adults with their marketing, that helped make consoles a more acceptable and affordable way for adults to game.

PC's at that time too were very complicated with multiple Graphics Cards too complicating matters further. Microsoft entered the Console space to bring PC games to a more mainstream audience and establish their 'DirectX' API as a PC standard too - if its required for their Box, it will be used for their Windows PC too - so neglected their PC platform to establish their 'Xbox' Console.

#4076. These 8+ PS5 Games Will Be Delisted in November and December 2026

The end of the year is always a prime time for PS5 game delistings and server closures, but fortunately we’re being spared a large list this year.

There are about eight titles with impending changes you need to be aware of, so here’s the full list:

Sony game Destruction AllStars will go completely offline on 25th November, following some alterations earlier in the year.

This will render most of the single player content unplayable, outside of a few arcade challenges, although the platform holder says your overall experience may be affected in those too.

In-game purchases will then be removed from Synduality: Echoes of Ada, the Bandai Namco live service shooter. This is the beginning of the publisher repurposing the game as a single player-only experience, with more changes planned in 2027.

PSVR2 MMO Zenith: Nexus will go offline on 18th December, and then the end of the year brings a slew of delistings, primarily from publisher GameMill.

This is due to licenses expiring for franchises like Avatar: The Last Airbender and Street Outlaws. If you purchase these games before they’re removed, they’ll remain in your library.

While it never officially released, PlayStation fans may want to pay attention to the impending closure of Ratchet & Clank: Ranger Rumble, which will be removed from mobile storefronts on 21st November.

One final thing to note is that 2K Sports will disable the online servers of NBA 2K25 on 31st December, but single player modes will remain.

That’s the full breakdown of everything being delisted in November and December 2026, then. I’ll update should any other announcements be made before the end of the year.

#4074. Splendid Junji Ito-inspired RPG World of Horror is now 20% more horrible, thanks to a free PC update with extra gods, locations, and wounds

This hole was already made for me, but now it's a fair bit wider and deeper

Excellent apocalypse RPG World of Horror has just received a sizeable free update, As Below So Above, adding no less than two Old Godly invasions for you to identify and thwart. One of these additional cosmic disasters involves four cults summoning their fave abominations at the same time. I picture them forming a shaky barbershop quartet on the skyline, while stamping the streets to mush. Damn it, Ath-Yolazsth – you're leading again!

Also in As Below So Above: more "enemies, mysteries, characters, items, spells, curses, and injuries", together with "a large batch of quality-of-life features and bug fixes". I can only applaud the vicious disconnect of listing "injuries" alongside "quality-of-life". These will be the most polished and ergonomic grievous wounds you've ever had! The experience will flow like your gushing blood!

This is the Junji Ito-inspired game's largest update yet, according to developers panstasz and publishers Ysbryd. It makes the game 20% bigger, though surely no mere percentage can ever encapsulate the creatures and forces that slumber on the other side of the mortal veil.

"Two never-before-seen manifestations of the Old Gods raise the stakes," explains the press release. "IKT-YOSIS, THE FIRST NIGHTMARE, sleeps in a gargantuan chamber beneath the mountains. With each ritual performed to wake him, the world above slowly reshapes itself and brings strange weather with it." You'll need to keep tabs on forecasts, if you want to get ahead of the elements. As for "THE WAR FOR SHIOKAWA", this "adds an extra level of terror, with four cults summoning their eldritch masters simultaneously to plunge the town into pure evil."

It's just as well there are three new puny human protagonists to continue the battle against these cyclopean trouble-makers: Kiriko, who knows her way around a Tarot deck, Satoshi, a seasoned hiker, and Makoto, a school AV club member. You'll also be able to enlist 10 additional allies and learn about them care of a reworked conversation system, which trips at random between investigations.

There's a new location, the Mountains, alongside 60 extra events, 19 enemies, three challenges, and 30 items. And let's not forget the Scenario Mode, which plays host to self-contained yarns set before the main game. The first of these Worldlets of Horror is a hunt for three students lost in the woods, with a variety of endings.

Lots of numbers! And while much of this may break your mind, none of it will break your mods. There's a new modding system that's backwards compatible with everything made for the 1.0 version.

Unfamiliar with World of Horror? Here is Alice Bee's review (RPS in peace): "Repetitive combat in World Of Horror can't entirely mar a unique, stylish and layered horror adventure that makes you want to play more the more that you play."

#4073. EA execs choosing Star Wars Battlefront 3 over Mass Effect 5 was the main factor in BioWare's demise, according to report

Corporate chair shuffling and the Mass Effect studio's recent struggles may also have played roles

The postmortem on BioWare, following their shuttering by EA this month, points to the publisher's preference to back Star Wars Battlefront 3 over Mass Effect 5 as the main factor in the demise of the beloved RPG developer. That's according to Bloomberg, who also report that a couple of other factors likely also had some influence.

The Bloomberg report paints EA's position as being one of a company caught between spending a bunch of money on a Star Wars shooter-shaped rock and a hard place with a sign that read Mass Effect 5. Disney reportedly swooped in to offer the publishers the opportunity to make Star Wars Battlefront 3 around the time EA were, as a result of being saddled with debt as part of the leveraged buyout which saw the Saudi government and private equity take them over, looking to not to spend as much cash.

So, Star Wars and Mass Effect became a decision of whether Star Wars or Mass Effect would be the better bet to stick projected hundreds of millions of dollars on. The suits, quelle surprise really, went for the series that currently sits just below powerhouse money-maker Winnie the Pooh on Wikipedia's list of the highest-grossing media franchises. Battlefront 3's development reportedly hasn't even kicked off yet, but it's got that safe and predictable big name to it, and will be a shooter to nestle among EA's treasured flotilla of gun and ball games, rather than an RPG.

Bloomberg add that that BioWare's well-documented up and down record with game releases since Mass Effect: Andromeda began a skid which Anthem only made worse and Dragon Age: The Veilguard couldn't arrest also played a role. Potentially also in the mix was some corporate chair and nameplate switching among EA's execs this summer, which saw EA Sports-linked suits David Tinson and Cam Weber promoted while reported BioWare advocate Laura Miele was sidelined via promotion from overseeing EA's non-sports studios to a gig based around helping big boss Andrew Wilson pursue "strategic growth opportunities beyond EA's core business".

For what it's worth, an EA spokesperson told Bloomberg the company "collectively" decided to shoot BioWare into space "following months of planning, review, and analysis, including careful consideration of evolving business conditions, industry dynamics, and our long-term priorities".

And so, BioWare's body has been sent to the stars, while Respawn and DICE look set to make Battlefront 3. There is a bit of depressing irony in EA deciding to go for the perceived safe bet of a big name licensed game over taking some risk on a game that'd come without Disney as a rights-holding middleman. This is, after all, the company which in 2022 ditched governing body Fifa as the namesake and licensing partner of their very successful football games, choosing the risk of going it alone with a lesser brand EA would have more direct control over and ownership of rather than sticking with an established big name juggernaut.

Then again, you could probably call EA's soccer games something like 'Hey, you, person reading this: the (insert year here) football game you're looking at thinks your face is ugly and your haircut's stupid' and they'd still fly off the shelves.

#4071. Wooshy wuxia actioner Phantom Blade Zero is sharp enough on the Steam Machine, if blunted on the Steam Deck

It would appear that Phantom Blade Zero (Phantom Blade 0? Zero? Let’s go with Zero) demanding more gigs than a mismanaged stadium is doing little to stop people playing the thing. It therefore stands to reason at least some folks will want to run S-Game Studio’s lightly Soulsy sword-em-up on the Steam Machine, so let us now examine how said GabeCube stands up to its effects-heavy martial artistry. With some settings proposals, natch.

Two signs boded poorly, before I got to testing the Machine. The first was a comment on Oisin’s day one patch piece, warning of heavy glitching on a Linux system. The second was my Steam Deck OLED, also a Linux system, being incapable of running Phantom Blade Zero at even close to a steady 30fps; even with the Low preset and some nasty-looking Ultra Performance upscaling, the game’s flashy moves and jerking (apologies – cinematic) camera shifts made for regular framerate drops into the teens.

Fortunately, the Steam Machine is much more resilient, even if it does benefit from a few quality cuts (and, realistically, will struggle if pushed beyond standard 1080p.) The Medium preset and Quality-level FSR are enough for 45-60fps in what I’ve played so far, and the High preset – while a touch susceptible to sub-40fps dips for my liking – is at least playable without major bugs or stuttering.

Strangely enough, the only major technical problem I’ve had wasn’t caused by graphics, or the Linux-based SteamOS, but the Steam Controller I was playing with. Despite being assured during the boot process that I was being treated to the Official Gamepad Configuration – cor! – an unresponsive map-opening button left me immobile during a prompt tutorial. Immobile and, I suppose without a map, lost. It turns out this this is a common bug with the Steam Controller specifically, and can be fixed by remapping the Select button, in SteamOS’s controller settings, to emulate the effect of clicking the touchpad of a PS5 pad. PC gaming.

With that sorted, Phantom Blade Zero seems to work fine? If I was nitpicking I’d point out that some high-drama sequences are visibly less buttery than the slower, roaming sections, which can exceed 60fps on Medium. Same for a lot of cutscenes, which aren’t hard-locked to 30fps like prerendered scenes often are, but do cause heavy framerate drops for little apparent reason. Still, it’s reasonable when actually playing.

Settings-wise, that Medium preset (with FSR on Quality) works well if you’re lazy. But a few of Phantom Blade Zero’s individual quality options aren’t terribly performance-sapping by themselves, and than thus be tuned upwards for a slightly nicer-looking wuxia tale with minimal drawback. Have a crack with the following:

Don’t miss those Dynamic Resolution Quality and Super Resolution Output Scale tweaks; on their defaults, they both make the game uglier than it needs to be. And on the subject of Super Resolution, FSR upscaling does leave a bit of roughness on certain edges, but then at 1080p, so does FSR even when it’s on its Native Resolution setting. You might as well get the extra frames.

#4070. Guide: GTA 6 Release Times and Preload: When Can You Start Playing?

Probably the most anticipated game of all time, GTA 6 is now less than two weeks away. As the launch draws closer, we're covering everything you need to know about its PS5 launch, including preload options and release times. In this GTA 6 guide, we cover the GTA 6 release times and preload.

On this page: GTA 6 Release Times and Preload: When Can You Start Playing?

Rockstar has confirmed GTA 6 will officially be playable from midnight on 19th November in your local time zone. As such, the game will unlock and be available first in New Zealand. If you preload the game, you'll be able to start playing GTA 6 as soon as it hits midnight on 19th November where you live.

If you pre-order the game, GTA 6 will be available to preload from 10th November. This is nine days before the game comes out, and was just brought forward two days by Rockstar.

Pre-ordering digitally means your preload should start automatically on PS5 as soon as it becomes available. The boxed physical version, which is just a code in the box, comes out on 12th November, the same day. You can redeem the code inside the case and start preloading the digital version of GTA 6 if you buy the game this way.

Rockstar has now officially confirmed the GTA 6 file size on PS5, and what you'll need to download, is 212GB. This is one of the biggest downloads and installs on console in history, and will probably only get bigger through patches and the addition of GTA Online.

GTA 6 will unlock and be playable in New Zealand first, as it's located in one of the furthest along timezones. The chances are New Zealand is further along in the day compared to wherever you live in the world, so yes, New Zealand will be the first to gain access to GTA 6.

Because of this, there's been a rising trend in people creating New Zealand PSN account to play games as soon as possible. This can be done with GTA 6 too, but you'll need to set up a fresh New Zealand PSN account and buy the game through its PS Store.

When you have done, you'll be able to play GTA 6 a few hours ahead of other countries like the USA. Keep in mind, though, that you can't transfer your save data from the New Zealand account you set up to your normal profile.

GTA 6 is available digitally on the PS Store, or in a basic physical version that ships without a disc. The latter provides a code in the box that you redeem on the PS Store to get the digital version.

The two PS5 digital versions on offer are: Standard Edition and Ultimate Edition.

Ultimate Edition / Ultimate Edition Upgrade Contents:

Rockstar is only selling GTA 6 in a digital format; you can't buy the game on a physical disc in any way. Even the version you buy in retail shops or from online retailers won't contain a disc. Instead, the actual GTA 6 box will have a code inside you can use to download the game. There's no version with a physical disc of any kind.

Rockstar has now confirmed a GTA 6 map will be made available, but it won't be included in the physical versions like for previous games. Instead, a physical GTA 6 map will be put on the official Rockstar store for $0.99. Or, it'll be included for free in all other purchases from the storefront.

#4069. Roblox users have made a playable version of Counter-Strike and full, working PlayStation games that you can play right now

Multiple remakes of beloved games including Counter Strike, The Simpsons: Hit and Run, and Super Hot, are available to play on Roblox right now. These have not been uploaded by the original game's creators.

One game - which is listed as an 'experience' in Roblox parlance, has been released by Roblox user Takeoff Interactive and listed as 'just a passion project', is a game "inspired by Counter-Strike" and has no monetisation according to its description. Eurogamer played this game today, and it looks and plays exactly like Counter-Strike.

The game includes the standard bomb diffusion mode, where two teams fight over two bomb sites. There are missing sound effects, the smoke doesn't look as good, and a friendly bot stabbed me in the back while diffusing a bomb, but otherwise it looks to be a largely identical recreation of Valve's game, albeit without Valve's involvement.

As for the PlayStation Experience, it's a full working PlayStation 4 dashboard with a media gallery, web browser, and trophies. There's even a server-based chat feature, in which Roblox players can talk to each other. The dashboard includes seven playable games - most of which are indie games. These include: The Simpsons Hit and Run, Cluster Truck, Superhot, Gang Beasts, Five Nights at Freddy's, Undertale, and PaRappaTheRapper.

Eurogamer played The Simpsons Hit and Run, and likewise found it to be a largely identical recreation of Activision's game. Players can drive around Springfield and cause mayhem much like the original game, albeit with a slightly dodgy objective guidance arrow.

Eurogamer also played Superhot, which once again looks and plays much like the original game, though it's not quite as visually impressive. This version of Superhot, Simpsons Hit and Run, and the PlayStation Experience as a whole was uploaded to Roblox by user Redwing Works, not Activision, not the Superhot team, and not Sony.

It is worth noting these are not Roblox games that are merely inspired by popular releases outside its ecosystem. Previously, a few popular Roblox games inspired by the game but not openly copying it exist. Counter Blox, for example, is a tactical FPS which uses Roblox assets and models, while Arsenal is another FPS inspired by Counter-Strike's Gun Game mode in which each kill progresses you to different weapons.

This is not the first time a popular game has been recreated on Roblox without the permission of its creators. The Peak developers urged people to pirate their game rather than play a "microtransaction-riddled ripoff slop" on Roblox.

Eurogamer has contacted Sony and developers for comment.

#4068. Warframe's fantasy-pilled sister Soulframe finally goes open to all this November, though Digital Extremes are "nervous" about certain changes

They're celebrating the end of closed alpha by poisoning the world

Warframe creators Digital Extremes have announced that their free-to-play fantasy RPG Soulframe will be available for everyone to download on 6th November, after two years in closed alpha. Finally, you serfs without "prelude" keys will be able to fire up Soulframe.com and make sense of my ranting about the sleeping animals on the lobby screen.

The new "open prelude" will land shortly before the game's 17th major update, Verse of the Veilands, which lets you grow your Omen wolfpup allies into rideable adult wolves by finding the ingredients for a special biscuit. More importantly, prelude 17 violently rearranges the game's wistful world, adding an Ubisoft-esque region purging system that is designed to guide new players a bit more emphatically towards the game's "votives". Aka, missions. Yes, Digital Extremes sort of have a bespoke term for every game feature in Soulframe. I find this can be either charming or maddening, depending on how much sleep I've had.

Here's how the region purging will work: after completing the game's Tormented Stag quest, you'll find that the landscape is being corrupted by siphons deployed by the villainous star-faring Ode faction. You have to complete votives to build energy and learn the sacred song of each region, allowing you to cleanse it and restore the environment.

In a roundtable preview session last week, creative director Geoff Crookes and lead designer Scott McGregor expressed a certain amount of anxiety about deliberately polluting Soulframe's fairytale ambience. "Scott and I were just talking yesterday about, aesthetically, how nervous we are about this change," Crookes commented, "because the game has gotten a lot of really great feedback on how cosy it is, how beautiful the world is, and you're going to enter a game that is much more unforgiving and harsh at first glance."

That said, he thinks the shift "pairs really well with going into open alpha, because it is a much stronger breadcrumb [trail] for the player, to pull them into the world and give them a bit more ownership of what they're doing." Once rinsed of Ode siphons, regions will appear more like how they are in previous versions of Soulframe, with activities such as fishing and new resources to snaffle.

McGregor added that hitherto, a lot of Soulframe players have gotten lost and put the game down after completing the opening "Fables", or story quests. "It's a really big change to the structural flow of the game, you know," he told the assembled journorabble. "We're very open and discoverable, and we had a lot of player feedback that was basically 'what do I do next? What do I do next? I don't know what to do next'.

"So [it's] taking that and mashing it with the votive system, which is our mission system for the game, and making that more of a directed experience," he went on, "and then once they get through that directed experience, they can go back to that open world." Prelude 17 will also let you accept votives more straightforwardly from the world map, after finding the local representative or mission giver.

Digital Extremes have a new Soulframe "pact" or character loadout on the boil, the Ode Shrike. It's a dastardly poacher class who specialises in spike traps and throwable bolas. The Shrike's standout ability is a balloon dart that lets you hoist enemies into the sky, as in Metal Gear Solid V.

You can read more about Soulframe's on-going reinventions on the official site. While you won't need a key to get access as of Nov 6th, the game's paid Founders program will remain the same. Digital Extremes will likely still run closed preview builds alongside the "open prelude", testing out features with a smaller group of players. They're also looking into giving you the ability to reset your character, so you can check out any new material added to parts of the game you've finished.

I'm not sure I've ever been exhilarated by Soulframe, but I like the poise, flamboyance and gentle complexity of its combat. I also really enjoy its faded tapestry aesthetics, though I think it's yanking on the goo-goo glands too avidly with all these fluffy forest animals. Enough photogenic wolfpups, Digital Extremes - let's see you make, I don't know, a blobfish look adorable.

It's also very interesting as a new live service project from a company defined by the success of Warframe. I spoke to the Soulframe developers earlier in the year about the challenge of borrowing Warframe's thunder without getting lost in its shadow.

#4067. Talking Point: What Are You Playing This Weekend? (November 7-8)

Anything you need to complete before...y'know?

Just two more weekends to get stuck into the games you're likely to abandon come November 19th.

It's been a fairly chill week for new releases with ZERO PARADES: Director's Cut the only notable launch (at least in my opinion). Hopefully something from our Deep Discounts sales roundup, or Xbox's Free Play Days titles are worth a shot.

Alrighty then, let's get into it. Here's what we're playing on Xbox this weekend:

I think I'm in need of a nice, feel good weekend of gaming. I'd like to play stuff that leaves me feeling all warm and fuzzy. It's appropriate timing, really, considering just how quickly it's getting dark now that the clocks have changed here in the UK.

Top of the agenda is starting The Wolf Among Us Remastered. I claimed the original version with Games with Gold, yet I've still not managed to boot it. Somehow, I've managed to avoid all spoilers in the thirteen year stretch. All I know is there's a pig called Colin or something. Anyway, I'm very excited to finally play it, as I've only ever heard good things about it.

Another game I'd like to experience for the first time is It Takes Two. My lady love and I are looking for our next co-op adventure after completing Split Fiction, so what better choice than Hazelight's other phenomenal game?

Oh, and if I get time, I'd also like to check out Routine. It isn't exactly giving warm and cosy vibes, but I'm worried it could leave Xbox Game Pass soon, and with GTA 6 on the horizon I don't have spare funds floating around.

I've got quite a lot going on this weekend, so I don't expect to be playing too much. Hopefully I might be able to fit in some more Star Wars Galactic Racer and Tape to Tape though - both of those games are so incredible!

Final Fantasy VII Remake Intergrade on Xbox Game Pass is also something I'm planning to spend a lot of time with, possibly when I go on holiday in a few weeks' time. I played the demo and loved it, so now it's time to try the full thing!

It's become a long-running joke that Warhammer 40K Blood Angels fans keep getting ignored or neglected, but that could be due to change early next year.

In a surprise announcement on Warhammer Community, the team revealed that Codex: Blood Angels would be arriving as of spring 2027 alongside an undisclosed number of new Warhammer 40K models. Yes, this could end up being yet another snub with a character or two like before. But specific wording in the announcement makes me hope it'll be a bigger drop. The title promises "Big news for Blood Angels," after all. It also points out that "Alongside [the Codex] will be new miniatures." Miniatures, plural.

However, That same post provided a look at the first new model; the returning Sanguinary High Priest Corbulo, bearer of the Red Grail and seen strutting his stuff in the image above.

Although there haven't been any bespoke Blood Angels models for a while, the faction has been a big focus of the current 11th Edition. Indeed, they were the poster-army for the Armageddon box set (which you can currently grab for 15% less at Amazon).

I'll admit, I could be applying clown makeup to myself right now or injecting copious amounts of hopium. Especially because last edition offered crumbs and even the upcoming Christmas Blood Angels Battleforce (which has just been announced) was a very weak entry, even compared to other boxes dropping at the same time. But making such a song and dance about this new Blood Angels launch, and their prominence in the current Warhammer 40K edition, make me hope they'll enjoy the same treatment the Dark Angels got at the beginning of 10th Edition – new heroes and troops alike.

It won't just be Blood Angels enjoying reinforcements either; spring will apparently bring us new releases for "Xenos, Chaos, and non-Space Marine Imperial armies." Could that be when we'll receive the long-promised Steel Legion revamp?

For now, we'll just have to wait and see. As it stands, one of the last major launches of the year looks to be Kill Team: Armageddon and its kick-ass Legion of the Damned.

#4065. "This is a serious incident" - Kingdom Come: Deliverance developer Warhorse suffers cyberattack

Studio working to determine "full extent".

Kingdom Come: Deliverance developer Warhorse Studios has confirmed it's suffered a "serious" cyberattack, saying it is currently working to determine the "full extent" of its impact.

"To our players and friends," a statement by the studio read. "We're sorry to share that Warhorse Studios has been hit by a cyberattack. We're working with cybersecurity specialists to secure our systems and understand the full extent of what happened. Thank you for standing with us." The message was released at 11am GMT and there hasn't been an update from the studio since. We've separately asked the studio if there have been any developments.

Warhorse CEO Martin Frývaldský discussed the incident in a Czech report (translated by DeepL), saying, "This is a serious incident for Warhorse Studios and for everyone affected. Our immediate priority is to secure our systems, determine the full extent of the breach, and take all necessary steps to protect our employees, partners, and our community. We are devoting all necessary resources and capabilities to resolving this situation."

Warhorse is currently working on two games, including a prestigious open-world Middle-earth role-playing game, based on Tolkien's legendary The Lord of the Rings fiction. It's also developing "a new Kingdom Come adventure", which we assume to be Kingdom Come: Deliverance 3. In addition, it's collaborating on a Kingdom Come: Deliverance film.

#4064. What are we all playing this weekend?

My scares should have been reserved for today, what with it being All Hallows' Eve and all, but my fright came on Thursday.

It was a dark October night and I was returning from work. A storm had blown through earlier in the week, so the evening was unusually crisp and clear. I walked between the terrace houses, feeling the eyes of work-from-homers on my back. I turned the key in the door to the communal hallway, climbed the creaky stairs, and tried to keep my footsteps light as I passed my rude neighbour's flat. My head was wholly absorbed by the prospect of the risotto I had waiting in the fridge/

I unlocked my front door and started up the internal staircase to the kitchen, not even bothering to turn on the lights. Out of the dark, something jumped down the stairs at me, hitting me in the stomach. I flicked the lights on in a panic and saw a small brown thing with a long tail bolting back up the staircase. A mouse. In my house.

Terrifying stuff, I'm sure you will agree. It almost put me off my risotto. Anyway, this is what the rest of the team will be up to this weekend..

OllieI've settled into a very comfy rhythm of playing the latest Trackmania campaign and also a bit of Factorio, both with my brother. When I've a bit of time to myself I'm also interested in trying out Queen's Domain. Heard good things!

JeremyI continue to chip away at our Castlevania walkthrough as it chips away at my soul. Such is the transactional bargain of dealing with Dracula during Halloween, no? However, as I answer the door for trick-or-treaters, I may partake in what is becoming an annual tradition - watching an old game playthrough on YouTube as I hand out sweets. I'm thinking I will watch the 1994 SNES game Nosferatu this year, which is not related to Castlevania but does feature a bold guy going to beat up Dracula and all of his minions with nothing but his feet and fists.

JamesMy previously mentioned attempts to play Mortal Shell 2 have been thwarted this week by, in chronological order, work, social obligations, brownie making, Deep Rock Galactic, and more brownie making. We go again.

EdwinI'm helping with a house move this weekend, so I doubt I'll have much time for your foolish computer entertainments, but I'd like to crack on with Queen's Domain and also, try out Danchi Days, a sorrowful comedy about trying to revive a summer festival in a 2000s-era Japanese neighbourhood.

CallumSuspiciously, Callum has been making squeaking noises in meetings. Is this a sign he planted the mouse? Perhaps he was the mouse. Surely, it's not a coincidence. There's no such thing as coincidence when it comes to mice.

MarkI want to finish Virtue and a Sledgehammer, having started it the other night. I really dug The Cosmic Wheel Sisterhood, one of Spanish studio Deconstructeam's previous games. Thus far, VaaS is hitting just as hard in terms of emotional beats, but in a manner that's more haunting than charming. We'll see where I land on it by the end.

JulianAs well as searching my flat for mouse hidey holes, I will be (touch wood/cross fingers/make a sacrifice to Bob the Builder) finishing the DIY I started last weekend. Alcove bookcases and a painted living room are in my future, I just have to manifest it.

Besides that, I've been dipping my toes into Titanium Court. I like it but I don't so far love it. It's witty, the presentation is excellent, but I feel like it is also keeping me at arm's length and I want to be drawn into its world, not kept at a distance. It may just need more time. I will also be trying hard not to sweep the moon.

And you, reader dear, what are you playing this weekend…?

#4062. GTA 6 is a massive 210GB download on PlayStation 5

There wasn't really any chance Grand Theft Auto 6 wasn't going to be a big download. Thanks to some new information, though, we now have a hard number.

PlayStation Game Size, which tracks PS Store game releases by poking through its backend, has revealed that GTA 6 has a chonky 210GB download size. While the actual space it's going to occupy on your console's SSD may be smaller, everyone will have to download over 200GB to play Rockstar's latest.

It's unclear whether GTA 6 is going to require a day one patch on top, or if it's already included in the 210GB. Given the interest in the game, the same PS Store sleuths will no doubt return to update us if the file size changes.

GTA 6 is expected to be one of the most dense games ever in sheer content. It has a highly-detailed, massive open-world map featuring a big number of side activities beyond what most contemporary games offer. The cinematic, hours-long story is the other element that contributes to that massive file size.

More broadly, while 210GB is a lot, it's not that much more than some of the biggest games on PS5. Call of Duty, for instance, is famous for its gargantuan file sizes when you have multiple modes installed - though in that case, at least, you're able to selectively uninstall the parts you don't play. This might prove tricky for GTA 6 if / when GTA Online arrives, as most of that is built on single-player content, the same map and so on and may not be easy to separate.

Not too long left now. GTA 6 arrives 19th November on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. Pre-loading begins 12th November, and hopefully that's enough time for everyone to finish that download.

#4061. Horror-steeped card game Forbidden Solitaire shows how a strong theme can elevate even decade-old mechanics

Like a tag team of oiled snakes that have entered a wrestling contest, theme is a difficult quality to pin down. A game can be well designed, but if it lacks a coherence between those mechanics and its appearance, narrative, and its framing, there is a dissonance that can be hard to ignore. I realise I've just stepped into an old argument by using the word 'dissonance', but Hocking was right, games that don't cohere can be jarring. A developer may desire that sensation of discomfort, but often it is accidental and unwanted.

Have You Played? is an endless stream of game retrospectives.

(Much like opening an article with a simile about wrestling snakes when there is nothing connecting that image to a game about solitaire. It might be a good line, but it doesn't smoothly connect with the rest of the article to elevate its argument.)

Anyway, what does this all have to do with Forbidden Solitaire, a game in which you're delving deeper into a dungeon filled with horrors, progressing by clearing screens of cards? Well, it's an excellent example of how well-handled theming can raise a game into something more than its parts.

I've been playing Grey Alien Games' work since they released Regency Solitaire in 2015, and their games often revolve around the same core, Solitaire-inspired mechanics. Each level is a screen filled with stacks of playing cards, and you must clear the screen by picking cards that are one higher or lower than the one currently in your hand. In addition to standard playing cards, you may find padlock cards which can only be cleared with a matching key card, special cards that reshuffle all the stacks, or ones that change cards into suits or numbers that may help you. Except, in each of their games – Regency Solitaire, Shadowhand, Ancient Enemy, and now Forbidden Solitaire - the scenario for those mechanics changes, and in doing do, they show the power of recontextualising.

In Forbidden Solitaire, you're playing a game within a game. Although it's set in 2019, your character is playing a 1995 CD-ROM they found in a second-hand shop. It's one you vaguely remember from your childhood, if mainly for the controversy it caused at launch. The game sees you breaking into an old dungeon and exploring its depths. Each locked door that blocks you, labyrinth that puzzles you, or enemy that challenges you is tackled with the mechanics of Grey Alien Games' previous releases: screens of stacked cards to be cleared. Even familiar special cards, such as the one which shuffles all the cards before you, make a return. As you progress through Forbidden Solitaire's dungeon, you're interrupted by messages from your sister in the present, who is researching the game and the controversy surrounding it, sending you links to police reports, old news clips of the secretive developer, and hidden documents on a centuries-old group of cultists.

Yet, despite the mechanical familiarity, it's this fresh theme that elevates Forbidden Solitaire into something special. For new players, the 1995 game framing device immediately gives an allowance for the simple card mechanics, and allows them to sink into the kitsch horror story of cult members developing haunted video games. But, for returning players like me, I can see all the neat ways the old tools have been adapted to fit this new world. When you find a person marked for sacrifice tied to a bed, for instance, the level to free them is filled with locks that only disappear when you match enough cards of the same suit. It's a pairing of unlocking mechanics that have been in Grey Alien Games' work for at least the past decade to a moment in the story where you are untying a character. The action dovetails with the narrative perfectly.

Anyway, when I realised the role that theme had to play in Forbidden Solitaire, I was feeling extremely smart and smug. Then I reread Adam (RPS in peace) and Pip's (RPS in peace) Regency Solitaire verdict from 2015.

Adam: I think the whole game is a superb example of how a decent design can be elevated by a strong theme. It’s not even particularly overindulgent - flourishes throughout but no extended dialogues or huge slabs of exposition. It’s a few attractive backgrounds (though with an inaccurate non-pebbled Brighton beach, I’m told by RPS chatroom stalwart and Brighton denizen Alec Meer), a handful of characters and miniature conversations to set the tone. But it’s all done so well. It seems to be aware of its own posture in a way that allows it to be well-mannered, well-meaning and not at all over-bearing.

If it had been pixies or space marines, I don’t think I’d have been particularly interested at all - and that’s not to say the actual card game isn’t well-constructed because it is - but even though the story is slight, it’s a great reward at the end of a few hands.

Pip: I'd agree with that, particularly about the setting. It's a game that has a good understanding of its own size, scope and the tone which suits it.

Those absolute cads. Still, go play Forbidden Solitaire anyway. It's a far better time than trying to get an oiled snake into a three-piece suit.

#4060. Rockstar Games employees have locked in a union vote next month, and it'll take place over Grand Theft Auto 6's release window

A date has been locked in for Rockstar Games employees to vote on whether to recognise their developer union. If successful, it will become the largest recognised union across the entirety of the UK video games industry.

The vote, which runs from the 12th to the 26th November, will give workers at Rockstar Games a chance to decide whether Rockstar will formally acknowledge and negotiate with the Rockstar Game Workers Union on matters involving its employees. These dates notably fall on either side of Grand Theft Auto 6's release date, and shortly after Rockstar's head of publishing Jennifer Kolbe told Bloomberg: "we go where the team goes. So if they want a union, they will have a union."

This announcement also comes as the legal battle between Rockstar and the Independent Workers of Great Britain union over the alleged unfair firing of over 30 employees. The union argues this was an attempt at union busting, whereas Rockstar stands by its decision to fire them for gross misconduct, pointing to the sharing of confidential information in a union Discord as the reason for the intervention.

This case was meant to have finished already. However, it ran long, resulting in its conclusion being delayed to the 17th and 18th of November.

So it's fair to say, November is a big month for Rockstar and its employees. It's entirely possible that by December, developers at the gaming giant will have both a union representing them and an industry shaking release to celebrate. Fingers crossed.

#4058. The Sunday Papers

Sundays are for looking upon my DIY works and despairing. Strewn sawdust, spilled paint, and hunks of broken MDF litter my living room kingdom. When will it be over? When will I be free? When will I be able to reassemble my sofa, sit down with a cup of tea in hand, and admire my books, unpacked and arranged on perfectly fitted alcove bookshelves?

The Sunday Papers is our weekly roundup of great writing about (mostly) videogames from across the web.

"Today?" I whisper hopefully in response to a paragraph of rhetorical questions. "Probably not," snaps back Reality. Especially if I don't get out of bed soon. Still, here in bed I can read the best writing about and not about games from the past week.

Inside our Gchat walls, there is a growing exhaustion with genAI stories. Every day another gaming boss talks about the inexorable march of the tech before putting out a trailer filled with blurry text and six-fingered characters. I don't doubt the tech is getting better, but it's not inevitable. As such, Rob Fahey's latest GI column is something of a balm:

There is currently a concerted and not-so-subtle campaign underway to try to manufacture consent for the use of AI in game development.

At its core, this is about presenting AI as a fait accompli. Every week or so we get a new report making dubious claims about almost every development studio already using AI. The message to developers is "you'll be left behind if you don't use it too"; to players, it's "this is already done and there's no turning back". Consume like good little consumers. Shut up and eat your slop.

A further tonic comes from Merritt K, who writes for Aftermath about the technological improvements rolling through Karaoke.

Doesn't it feel like everything — especially everything Big Tech touches — is getting worse? Generative AI, not merely content with robbing humans of our craft and jobs, has escaped containment into physical reality in the form of shitty event flyers and small business signage. Hugely profitable industries like video games and film are being torn apart by the financialization of the economy as shareholders seek ever-increasing short-term profits. Algorithmic pricing of rent and groceries threatens to further punish the working class for the crime of not being born rich.

But in the heart of despair, we must reach for that which is good and pure and — dare I say it — better than it used to be. Karaoke is one of those things. And it is better not because of the disruption of tech giants, but, as is often the case, thanks to the work of enterprising maniacs toiling in obscurity, purely out of the love of the game.

I've been playing Forbidden Solitaire this week, where FMV sequences starring Xalavier Nelson Jr as an obsessive fantasy-author-turned-video-game-developer are played for laughs. So it was with a minor sense of whiplash I read Ashley Bardhan's piece for This Week In Video Games. Bardhan speaks to horror developers inserting themselves into FMV games to confront and explore violence against women.

Cara Cadaver uses her own photos and videos to represent multiple victims of sexual violence and murder in her unflinching 2025 game Vile: Exhumed. She tells me over email, “Being a woman is inherently a horrifying and violent experience, any way you slice it. One of my inspirations for making games in general is pulling from real-life experience and telling stories that most every woman has lived in some way; that’s real horror.”

“Horror in general has been a major outlet for me while dealing with trauma, and so much of horror as a genre goes back to women,” Cadaver says. “Women’s stories belong in horror — and that has been the case as long as horror has existed.”

Over at RPS-but-it's-The-Fade, Brendan's run through what made Bioware games great (and also terrible).

Bioware established romance as a must for any blockbuster RPG worth its frost salts (and not just RPGs).

Kissing your friends on the mouth is everywhere in mainstream and indie games today. It's a verb now. Characters are "romanceable". I played Nivalis Nights last month and could not get away from the swarms of horny NPC citizens trying to jump my noodle serving bones. Baldur's Gate 3 launched with a bug that made your companions fuckable in just a few nights, and people didn't even notice. They thought: that's normal and right, I should shag everyone, gender and orientation be damned. See that mountain? You can fuck it. And that's (at least partially) thanks to Bioware.

GTA is an unignorable thing. It is one of those breakout cultural objects that has its own gravity, drawing in attention and comment from politicians, mainstream press, parents, schools, comedians, columnists, footballers, taxi drivers, and hairdressers. In all the weight of it, I hadn't yet really seen it as a game. Simon Parkin's Edge cover feature may not reveal many new details about the game but it has made me appreciate it as a game (and maybe even get a little bit excited for its eventual PC release.

Nelson, grave-faced but friendly, wearing all black, with grey-flecked stubble, settles into a leather-and-chrome Eames chair while we perch on a burnt-orange sofa facing a pair of expansive wall-mounted TVs. In the past, Rockstar has carefully stage-managed encounters such as this. For previews of previous GTAs, one team member played the game while a publicist read from a pre-prepared script, further evidence of the paranoia that can take hold when an artist is working on something the entire world is desperate to see.

Today, however, Nelson has no script and, apparently, no plan. For the next 90 minutes he simply plays the current build, following his nose, confident that the game's systems will hold together wherever he pushes them, that this world's glories will glint and shimmer no matter which angle he approaches from. It is an extraordinary demonstration not of paranoia but of trust – in the game, in the team that built it, perhaps even in us.

Nelson picks up the controller and lets Grand Theft Auto VI speak for itself.

I am guilty of forgetting and looking away, but the humanitarian crisis in Gaza has not ended, it is deepening. Writing for the LRB, Selma Dabbagh bluntly captures the ugly events of the past two years :

In January 2025 Donald Trump described Gaza as a ‘demolition site’. ‘You’re talking about probably a million and a half people,’ he said, ‘and we just clean out that whole thing.’ The number is closer to two million people – not a ‘whole thing’ but two million individual human beings – who have been driven into an area that’s less than a third of the densely inhabited land they lived on. Their cities and arable lands – palms, olives, coriander, citrus and pomegranate trees – have been obliterated.

I'd like there to be a big reason for this week's music recommendation, but really it's just a little victory lap. I managed to nab some tickets to see This Is The Kit, so give Bashed Out a listen, yeah?

Welcome back to Conformity Gate. With Stranger Things Day sending us all back to the Upside Down today, Sony has the headphones to pair with that world-saving Walkman. The brand has just announced a Stranger Things edition of the new MDR-3R wired headphones, now available with bold red cushions (and a black set included in the box). The $79 / £59 Stranger Things variant bumps up the price of the new release a little (the standard model starts at $59 / £49) but maintains a style fit for Hawkins.

The Sony MDR-3R headphones are being described as "Newtro" by the brand, combining more modern audio handling (and a USB-C connection) with the instantly recognizable retro aesthetic. Sony has faithfully reconstructed the MDR-3 design, with that skinny band, chunky silver driver plate, and simple design. If we ever needed another reason to start running up that hill, this is it.

The new Sony MDR-3Rs are still waiting to go live on the brand's own site, though notifications are available if you want to be one of the first in the line. It's worth noting that the red-cushion Stranger Things version is a limited edition, so keep that refresh button warm.

So what does the Stranger Things edition bring to its higher price tag? It's a subtle one. The blue / orange cushion color options of the standard model are replaced with a deep Upside Down red and black pairing with a Stranger Things logo stamped at the top of the headband.

If you're going for the full '80s aesthetic, you'd be better off with the orange base option, saving yourself some cash in the process. If you're going like-for-like with Max herself, you'll need the limited edition to get access to those black pads.

The headphones themselves are constructed from a lightweight aluminum and stainless steel, powered by that USB-C connection for a charge-free experience, and still feature an inline remote with an integrated microphone for media control and calls.

Sony says it's kept the MDR-3R sound profile as close to the original as possible, while still elevating sound with some more modern features. That open-back design is still going to give your music plenty more breathing space, but the brand has extended both lower and upper ranges for a more dynamic quality.

While the absence of that ninth episode still continues to hurt, at least we've got some tunes to see us through. Plus, with Maya Hawke joining the Magic: The Gathering movie there's still plenty from the series stars in the works.

#4055. "We need to understand what the need is here" - Arc Raiders studio still undecided about the future of PvE despite a seemingly successful test

"Perhaps this is more a signal that the game could support more player types."

Arc Raiders recently ended its first-ever test for a dedicated PvE mode, following months of player requests. While feedback has generally been favourable, developer Embark has gone quiet about whether the mode will return as a permanent addition.

There's a reason for that: Embark doesn't appear to have made a decision internally. Speaking to MP1st, executive producer Aleksander Grøndal said the team is currently looking through the data and there are several factors to consider.

"Now that we've concluded the PvE matchmaking toggle test, we're doing a deep dive into what that means," said Grøndal. "Of course, we were a bit skeptical about bringing such a mode to the game for historical reasons, but now we need to discuss what we want to do going forward."

The "historical reasons" Grøndal is likely referring to is the fact Arc Raiders started out as a purely PvE co-op shooter, before Embark pivoted during development and created the extraction PvPvE shooter we know today.

Since Arc Raiders' release, however, two different audiences emerged: players who love the uncertainty and higher stakes excitement PvP creates, and those who simply want to engage with the game's deep PvE mechanics without having to worry about other players.

"I think the game has an appeal in its nature and that a certain player type wants to play the game without the stress, you know? Perhaps this is more a signal that the game could support more player types, and we need to figure out how to support that," he explained.

The challenge, according to Grøndal, is creating something that caters to the two different groups of players "without undermining the premise of the game itself". To do that, Embark needs to find the PvE mode's true purpose.

"We need to understand what the need is here," Grøndal explained. "Is it more a chill side mode you can play between more intense PvPvE rounds? Is it more a challenge mode that you can test your skills against AI? Or perhaps it's a full experience with PvE only?"

Indeed, Grøndal previously said that offering two distinct modes for Arc Raiders' different audiences is a possible future for the game, so all options are seemingly being considered, even if the developer can't offer a concrete answer today. "All options will have different implications on how we build future game updates," Grøndal added.

Arc Raiders recently released its biggest update, Frozen Trail, which saw player numbers shoot up to highs the extraction shooter hasn't witnessed in six months.

I'm sure the artist formerly known as Prince would have loved it, at least

In this genAI world, every single leak that makes its way out into the world should be seen as more of a "leak" until proven otherwise. With that said, it does kind of seem like a remake of the first Persona game is on the way, with some footage supposedly leaking and showing it in action.

The leaked footage was shared yesterday to the GamingLeaksAndRumours subreddit, originally uploaded to the file-sharing site Gofile on Halloween, i.e. yesterday, i.e. October 31st. You will not at all be surprised to hear that, stylistically, it's incredibly in line with the vibe of contemporary Persona, a la the visual design established with Persona 5 that's been carried through to the Persona 3 and 4 remakes.

There's not a whole lot of footage to actually look at, just shy of two minutes all told. One bit shows the game's protagonist walking through a school at night before starting a battle. Again, the battle system looks like what you'd expect from Persona, being turn based and whatnot. The colour theme for this one is overwhelmingly purple, too, which at least lines up with the series' 25th anniversary artwork. What's perhaps slightly odd is that Persona 2's protagonist can be seen in battle; not sure if this is implying a combination of the two games, if two remakes are being made in tandem and it's a temporary use of assets, or if it's just an odd placeholder.

Persona 1 and 2 remakes wouldn't exactly be much of a surprise. Ashley interviewed series producer Kazuhisa Wada not too long ago, and he literally said "Persona 1 and 2 are something we’ll probably eventually do too." A knowing tease from Wada, perhaps? Either way, the gameplay on display here looks believable, and Sega's leakier than a broken faucet (various Persona bits have leaked in the past too), so, something to keep an eye on at the very least, even if best taken with a pinch of salt.

#4053. As Skydance merges with Warner Bros. and Paramount, the company offers voluntary redundancy and mandates return to the office

Skydance - the newly formed corporate megazord combining Warner Bros and Paramount - has issued a full five-day return-to-office mandate to employees, and offered voluntary buyouts as the merging of the companies begins.

The company was formed earlier this month following a much-debated $110bn Paramount acquisition of Warner Bros., in which both companies were squished together to be led by a refreshed board, which includes former UK prime minister Tony Blair (in an advisory role), philanthropist Laurene Powell, and former Activision CEO Bobby Kotick.

In an internal email seen by Vertical Slice, CEO David Ellison and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz told employees that in-person collaboration is "vital" for the company going forward.

"Especially in a creative company like ours, the best ideas come from people in the same room, sharing perspectives, challenging one another and solving problems," the email read. "Being together isn't just about showing up. It's about inspiring one another, learning and coaching, forming friendships and having access to the casual conversations that spark something great.

"With that in mind, we will adopt a five-day in-office policy across all of Skydance. We truly believe this is in the best interest of our company and our people. We've seen the benefits firsthand at Paramount, and we want every part of Skydance to share in them."

The voluntary buyouts, meanwhile - which for those who don't know is an opportunity for employees to leave the company with a severance package - were described as a "one time offer", though it was not clear which teams within Skydance are eligible to accept it.

Skydance now includes the gaming studios once under Paramount and Warner Bros. This includes the game studios Netherrealm (Mortal Kombat), Portkey Games (Hogwarts Legacy), Avalanche Software (not to be confused with Avalanche Studios), Paramount Games Studios, and various other WB studios. It is unclear whether developers at these studios have been offered the voluntary buyout, nor when their employees will have to return to the office.

Skydance is not the only company to have offered voluntary buyouts recently. This week Microsoft offered 60,000 of its employees the same deal - that's roughly 25 percent of its staff - amid sweeping Xbox layoffs and its big AI push. Last year, EA also introduced a return-to-office policy to its employees, with its CEO saying in-person work creates "a kinetic energy that fuels creativity."
